title: Brothers in Arms: Earned in Blood™
text: Earned in Blood, just like the other two Brothers in Arms games, has an amazing story. The three games combined are simply the greatest WWII games out there. Call of Duty 2, of course, was amazing for the African campaign. But Gearbox hold the title for recreating very important battles in the Normandy region in France. I mean, if you've played the games, then maybe you've seen the extras where pictures show how much detail they put into recreating the villages in Northern France. It's very remarkable. The story, you play as Joe Hartstock, Red, in this one. Maybe you remembered him in Road to Hill 30. Well, this game takes place alongside Road to Hill 30 as Joe is recounting his actions to SLAMarshall, a war documentarian, recording the actions of combat troops for the military. Throughout the story, Joe sees his friends get injured, change their attitude during the war, and some of them unfortunately die. But that's war. The audio design is unreal. My dad walked by when I was playing and noted how realistic the sounds were for the rifles and panzers. The soundtrack, too, is amazing. Basically, I'm biased as hell as I already love WWII anything, but the strong character development, friendship, and tactical elements make the Brothers in Arms games some of my favorites. 9.0/10

text: Earned in Blood is the second installment of the Brothers in Arms series. In this game you play as Joe Hartsock, one of the members of Sgt. Backer’s squad. In this game, you fight parallel to the story of Road to Hill 30 and get to see the story form another angle. Just like the first game, this one is still a slow paced, tactics based shooter with some of the draw backs from the previous game. No way to heal in battle, low weapons accuracy (although its more precise then it feels). Just like the other game, this title still contains a great story and top notch “horrors of war”. As I said in my review of Road to Hill 30, if you are looking for a run and gun shooter this game is not for you. It is, however, a well done tactics based war game with a story that pulls at the heart.

title: Brothers in Arms: Earned in Blood™
text: Even though this and RTH30 were made around the same time, I feel that, whereas RTH30 has a lot of good ideas but a flawed execution, EiB tightens almost all the faults of its predecessor and hits the mark its aiming for a lot more frequently. The gameplay itself is more-or-less identical to RTH30, but narratively it does something bold and actively undermines the perspective and heroics of the main character of the first game. In RTH30 you played troubled and occasionally whiney Matt Baker, and in EiB, his friend and occasional squadmate Red Hartsock. We see that Red's perspective of events differs quite strongly from Matt's, and that the character you played before wasn't viewed as quite the hero as the game made you feel. He is seen to be losing his mind and as such Red begins to distrust and even resent him. The dialogue feels a lot less clunky this time round, and the story hits the emotional peaks in a much stronger way. The sound effects are still fantastic and really immerse you in the battlefield, and the voiceover work is of better quality this time round, although there are small but noticable moments of lacking audio that lower your immersion and occasionally undermine the emotion of the moment. I felt like the level design of this game is superior to the first, and as such, I rarely felt like I was being funnelled into a kill-corridor in which you were damned no matter which path you chose. Searching for flanking routes and thinking outside the box is almost always rewarded, and allows you to feel like you're genuinely outwitting the enemy. There is the odd AI brainfart, which is at best funny when you shoot an enemy and he stand there like nothing happened, and at worst rage inducing as your teammates move to the outside of cover rather than finding a proper place to hide, but generally speaking the enemy AI is quite strong, and they'll shift and change cover in order to confront a flanking threat. Tonally the game is as dark as the first, and in its efforts to mimic the real feel of battle, the game is a sombre one. I feel rather harrowed now that it's done, and it makes a small but powerful effort to compliment the player's decision making when you keep your teammates alive. I think this is one of the best and most realistic-feeling WW2 games ever made, whilst also managing that fine balance that allows things to remain fun to play. I highly recommend this game, but you WILL need to have played the first one, in order to understand the story.

title: Bulletstorm: Full Clip Edition
text: As far as the actual gameplay goes, recommending Bulletstorm: Full Clip Edition is a no brainer. As far as recommending it as a remaster goes…well, we’ll get to that in a moment. Originally releasing in 2011, Bulletstorm was, and still remains, a wholly unique FPS experience. What made Bulletstorm stand out from the oversaturated FPS of the time was the unique mechanics that it possesses. The game features an energy whip or leash that allows the player to pull enemies towards you. When you do this, the enemy will stay in a suspended stasis of sorts, moving in slow motion while you and everything around you moves in real time. Coupled with this mechanic is the boot mechanic (thanks Dark Messiah!) that allows you to kick enemies. With these mechanics working in tandem, Bulletstorm creates a fast and frantic atmosphere that is just sheer joy to play. The guns work in perfect harmony with one another and each has its use in the game. Thankfully, you can switch your loadout pretty regularly, so it’s easy to tailor your weapons to the given situation. Thankfully the story doesn’t take itself too seriously because it’s definitely absurd and a bit over the top too. If you enjoy cheesy action films, then the dialogue of Bulletstorm is sure to put a smile on your face. This is also helped by the generally great voice acting. The revenge story of Bulletstorm is intriguing enough to pull you through to the finish, but it’s really all about the gameplay here. Along with Singularity, Bulletstorm remains one of the most criminally underrated games of the Xbox 360/PS# generation. Now, I tend to loathe using words like “underrated” but I think it really fits here. The developers People Can Fly created a real gem here, and it still holds up extremely well six years later. So I’ve gushed about the original Bulletstorm release enough, how is the remaster? Well, frankly, it’s not much of a remaster. I think that the original game still looks just fine and this Full Clip Edition makes it look slightly better, I guess. Some visuals are slightly crisper and it runs at a rock solid 60 FPS no matter what but it’s not a huge leap from the original. Also, make sure that you disable Cinematic Mode as I found that it severely washed out the colors. This leads me to my biggest gripe about the remaster: lack of graphics options. There’s barely anything there besides resolution and texture. It seems like there was not a lot of thought put into the graphical upgrade, which is a real shame because I think this game could have looked even better. As far as extra content goes, there’s a New Game Plus which lets you use all of the weapons from the start. This is a nice touch and will let you changeup a second playstyle. There are additional Echoes as well, which are basically score based challenges. Not my cup of tea, but they’re there if you want them. One of the most lauded additions was the Duke Nukem voice pack. Now, I’ve never particularly been a fan of the Duke, but I found the voice over to be frankly quite bad. It comes across as flat and just plain out of place. Based off pure gameplay, I think everyone should play Bulletstorm: Full Clip Edition. Based off the so-so remaster and lack of new content for a $60 game, I’d wait for at least a 50% sale. The game still holds up extremely well but I think that the asking price is a bit much for a six year old game at this point. Negatives of the remaster aside, I cannot emphasize enough how fun Bulletstorm is. I really do hope that the game does well enough that People Can Fly can make a long overdue sequel. Do yourself a favor and experience one of the best FPS from last gen (on sale of course).

title: Bulletstorm: Full Clip Edition
text: Bulletstorm: Full Clip Edition is the remastered version of the 2011 Shooter Bulletstorm, with some added extras. I’m a huge fan of the original game, so I was excited from the first moment on when I heard about the Full Clip Edition. So let’s get into it.  You play as Grayson Hunt, Ex-Leader of the so called Dead Echo Squad and now full time Outlaw, that is on the hunt for the guy that betrayed his Team years ago. But to be honest, Bulletstorm isn’t really the kind of game you play for the Story. It isn’t bad and it helps you do understand the motivation of your character and his buddys, so it does its job. But Bulletstorm is a game, you want to play for the…. And Bulletstorm has probably the most unique gameplay of any Ego-Shooter out there, and it is probably the only shooter in which you’ll think: “Shooting my enemies? Booooooring. Let’s see what I could do with them” Bulletstorm includes the so called “Skillshot” system. This system rewards you with points for killing your opponents in creative ways. For this, the game offers various ways and possibilities in every location you are, it all depends on your imagination and the guns you are having with you. And of course the environment. You have your main rifle with you all the time, and you can choose between 2 other guns to carry around at a time. Every weapon has a second, devastating, fire mode. For example: The sniper rifle will shoot explosive bullets which are also allowing you to move you enemies around for a bit after you hit them. The shotgun shoots Blastwave which will cremate everything in its way. With the points you earn, you can unlock new guns and upgrade them and restock your ammo if needed. The Skillshot system is what makes the game so much fun. You just enjoy every kill and find new creative ways all the time to get rid of your opponents till the end of the last level.  1. Campaign In four different difficulties from Very Easy to Very Hard. 2. If you finished the campaign once, you can replay it in the overkill mode, which allows you to carry every weapon at once and unlock unlimited ammo if you fulfil certain goals. 2. Echoes: It’s some kind of time attack mode. You can replay certain parts of the campaign and some unique level only made for the Echoes. Very fast and fun. 3. Overkill Echoes: Basically the same, but with various requirements’ you have to fulfill. 4. Multiplayer. Anarchy Modus: You get thrown in various smaller areas with up to 4 other players. The goel is to fight of wave after wave of enemies. The Multiplayer has some unique skillshots to it, which require the Players to work together. You unlock points, and can buy new weapons, upgrades or stats for your char with them after each round. Also you climb up in an overall level. With that you will unlock cosmetic stuff each for your character, like new armor, gun colors, win animations and so on. It’s fun for some hours but nothing you will play for weeks on end. For a game which was originally released in 2011 Bulletstorm still holds up great compared to modern games. Sure some effects aren’t the very best anymore, but some places will still make your chin drop. The effects are great, the weapons and Firemodes have a good feeling to them and you can really feel the carnage you’re are causing with your actions. In my whole playtime it happened twice to me that the game exit back to my desktop when I entered the main menu after launching the game. Otherwise I had a constant framerate for the whole time and no stutters or anything and Max settings. Also the loading times are really short. Thumps up for that. Bulletstorm - Full Clip Edition is a great and unique Ego-Shooter that offers you an experience like no other game of the genre. If you like Shooters just for a tiny bit, I can fully recommend this game to you. You won’t regret it. If you have already played the original, like I have, you have to decide for yourself if you want to buy game again, since it doesn’t offers that much more as the original. I personally don’t regret it. And if you never played the game yet, you are in for a ride you won’t forget anytime soon.

title: Bulletstorm: Full Clip Edition
text: Its like Brutal Doom in 3D. Its combat is almost one of a kind with the skillshots and environment. Enemies react marvelously to how you kill them. And there are so many ways how. Kick them into a cactus, a grinder, a thorn, an abyss. Or use the whip to get them close to fire your shotgun and see them fly again into a cactus or some other environmental death. What makes the gameplay really stand out is that you're constantly looking for spectacular ways to kill by positioning yourself properly to kick them into the right direction. The guns are great, I wont spoil it but trust me there's some really unique and cool guns that fit perfectly. They all also have an alternate firemode which adds that special something. Needless to say the graphics are gorgeous. Its the tiny details that I appreciate. Shoot them in the throat and they'll choke on their own blood. Shoot them in the groin and they'll hold their balls. Dismember them. Blow their head off. It does what many other games are too ashamed off.

title: Call of Cthulhu®: Dark Corners of the Earth
text: Decade old first person stealth. Trial and error gameplay. Clumsy first person shooting. Game breaking bugs that were never officially fixed by the developers, making the vanilla game you just purchased all but completely unplayable. The only way to (currently...) make the game run without crashing that I found was to download and install a fan-made patch , download and run video capture software called Bandicam , and also go into your video card settings to turn native V sync on. You probably want a walkthrough handy as well to make sure any problems you run into aren't bugs, and there are some solutions to puzzles that are not so much too difficult or counter-intuitive as you'll walk past key elements a hundred times due to muddy graphics or poor signposting. I say that as someone who is very anti-walkthrough in most cases, but trust me... unless you want to turn a ten hour adventure into forty hours of walking in circles use the ♥♥♥♥ing guide when you're stuck. Still with me? Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth is an excellent survival horror/adventure game and I highly recommend it. I had to start off with the negative points to put it into perspective: to get to the good parts of this game you're going to have to swallow some♥♥♥♥♥♥ but it's worth it. You play the game as Jack, a hardened, somewhat stereotypical detective of the Elliot Ness variety. It's 1930's American prohibition era New England, so take the tough guy attitude and film noir/Dragnet speak to the extreme, calmly making strictly factual observations about the world around you, even while being tortured with a car battery by J. Edgar Hoover or staring into the unspeakable eyes of fish monsters and ancient gods. In a game explicitly about Lovecraftian horrors and utter madness, the one note voice acting of Jack provides endless comic relief. Whether it's intentionally funny or not is up to debate. Nothing phases this guy... Jack is on the case of freeing a prisoner from the eerie, not-quite-right town of Innsmouth. The few sane inhabitants of the town warn him of cult activity and that the fishy smell that permeates the streets might have a more malicious point of origin than the cannery. What follows is quite an adventure into increasingly alien, hostile environments that is surprisingly ambitious in scope. While the first third or so of the game takes place in Innsmouth, you'll be boarding a Navy vessel under siege by Dagon's minions and exploring impressively sprawling, twisting caverns as well as an underwater city. If you just gasped and muttered, “Spoilers...”... The game is called Call of Cthulhu. Read some Lovecraft. The game is a true eclectic mix of genres: stealth, FPS, old school adventure and puzzle solving, exploration, what would be considered some light modern “survival” elements. You can converse with NPCs and complete optional side quests. This is a true jack of all trades, and like most times that cliché is used not many of the gameplay mechanics are “good” in the traditional sense. Stealth is unreliable and usually frustrating as enemies seem to spot or hear you when they feel like it. The weapons you get early on feel almost useless with either a random spread pattern and/or a cockeyed aim down sight perspective, but there are instanced where you are forced to fight. Good luck. The most consistent thread is the adventure elements where you're using items from your inventory to solve puzzles and combing the playspace for clues. Though, with some poorly placed checkpoints combined with the aforementioned shaky stealth and combat you'll have to repeat in many instances... see above for a walkthrough link. There are a few standout systems, most notably how the game handles health and sanity. When you take damage it is represented both by the bodily location of the wound and the type of injury. You might get grazed in the chest, which can be fixed by applying some bandages from the inventory of which you usually have plenty. Something deeper might require sutures to close a gash, otherwise you'll bleed out. If you fall from a good height you will break a leg (or two), and you'll physically limp, causing a sickening crunching sound and snail paced movement until you attach a splint. The healing items are all tracked separately so there's no Cure All to speak of save a shot of morphine which won't actually heal you, just provide temporary pain relief while you desperately search for a medkit. I really like this system: yeah, it's kind of goofy that Jack goes from a bloody mess with exposed bone and torn clothes to a-okay in five seconds, but it's the perfect compromise between nitty gritty hardcore micromanagement survival and typical hording. When you get injured or see anything particularly unnerving (which you will), Jack starts to lose his mind. He's no longer the monotone detective; as his vision distorts and he loses control he sounds convincingly terrified as he mutters to himself, questioning his sanity and his purpose and his will to go on. Sanity effects aren't new or rare for these games, but whatever filter they are using to convey being disorienting is extremely effective. Something as simple as looking down while descending a ladder brings out Jack's vertigo, and let him freak out for too long and you'll get a gut-churning empathetic feeling yourself. Again, I may sound overly negative when picking apart certain aspects of the game, but overall it rises above it's shortcomings. The janky, low budget nature can work in it's favor; you don't entirely trust the game to play by the rules. While not a jump scare/gorefest, it's does not shy away from generally taboo subjects: dead kids, an upside down take on beastialitality, torture, sacrifices, all that good stuff. Just when you're laughing at Jack's oblivious take on fishmen, you'll bear witness to something genuinely unsettling. When the game hits, it hits hard. And it's paced impeccably; curse repeating the same chase sequence all you want, once you go further down the rabbit hole there just seems to be a reason for everything. It's one of those games that you question why you're playing, but you can't stop. You have to see it through to the end, whether it drives you mad or not. Even the very last sequence took me many, many tries to the point where I was ready to give up and just watch the ending on YouTube and write a damning review about how broken the game is (and I already wrote one before taking the time to patch it), yet I persisted. And then as the credits rolled I just sat back and though, “What a great game.” It's fitting, I guess.

title: Call of Cthulhu®: Dark Corners of the Earth
text: Some horror games stand above all others in delivering a polished, terrifying experience.  Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth...is NOT one of those games.  This game is the definition of a buggy, terrible, unintuitive nightmare.  You will be scared, but not because of the lovecraftian nightmares chasing you, but because of the crap game itself. I picked this up on the recommendation of many people, who cited it's atmosphere and story as the selling points.  And, to be fair, the atmosphere is oppressive, nightmarish, and very unsettling, while the story is pretty decent, a nice introduction to lovecraft for those who haven't or don't want to read his writings, for whatever reason. HOWEVER!  This game has far too many problems for anyone to want to play.  First the control scheme is terrible.  For an FPS it's decent enough, but the controls require you to be nose to nose with an item or enemy before you can use it or attack it.  Also, the game is built like an FPS, but in the first half of the game, you are completely weaponless and defenseless...not very smart.  Second, the game is incredibly unintuitive.  Almost nothing is explained in terms of gameplay and nothing that you need to do is made clear.  Passages to the next section are buried in crawlspaces or hidden so well that 30 minutes of searching is required to even dream of moving forward.  It feels like a point and click adventure that was badly shoved into an FPS.  The gunplay and healing is different, as the weapons are from the 1920s and require manual reloads, like the shot gun which can only fire two shots before being reloaded.  The healing happens in real time, so you have to plan the where and when to heal.  That would be fine, but you die so easily from even the most minor of wounds and the aiming is so awful that enemies will FREQUENTLY kill you. And that's another thing.  The first time you try a section, your pulse will pound, your heart will race, and you'll feel really exhilirated because of how tense and scary it is.  The fifteenth time you try a section, you will want to scream at the screen for how buggy and unintuitive the section is.  The game loses its mystique of horror when you have to constantly reload saves to redo a section over and over again because of a mistake where you don't know what to do or don't know what you're doing wrong.  This game is so frustratingly unfun that I had to quite at one section where the glitches and poor game design just broke me.  One section of the game requires that you fire a cannon at 3 blue lights to trigger an event.  Problem.  There are NO BLUE LIGHTS.  The game's graphics are buggy and glitched so that sections like that are nigh on unplayable, and those are only for starters.  The platforming, yes there is platforming, is equally unplayable and unfun. The only reason at all to play this would be for the story, and for that, you can go to the youtubes.  Greatest horror game of all time my butt.  This game is a buggy mess.  Cthulhu and Lovecraft deserve better.  Stay far away from this piece of gargabe.

title: Call of Cthulhu®: Dark Corners of the Earth
text: Though the game is a little clunky and really doesn't like being minimized, I was actually quite enjoying this game. The game unfortunately suffers from one massively disasterous design flaw though; when you retry a section that you failed in, you have to watch the same curscenes again before you get back in for another swing at it. This may not sound like much, but it is awfully tedious to see and hear the same lines of dialogue over and over again, especially in a game that's progress is based around trial and error. If you can get past that, the clunky controls, and the odd design choices then give this a go, it has some nice atmosphere and has some interesting idea's for 2005/2006. Cutscene repetition is a crime against game play in my eyes, so I can't really recommend it myself.
